**Sūrat al-A'lā**
Nineteen verses, Meccan

﷽ (In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾ ﴿And who determined and guided﴾ ﴿And who brought forth the pasture﴾ ﴿And made it dark stubble﴾

﷽

﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾ ﴿And who determined and guided﴾ ﴿And who brought forth the pasture﴾ ﴿And made it dark stubble﴾ Know that the words of Allah, Exalted is He, ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ contain several issues.

**The first issue:** Regarding His words ﴿the name of your Lord﴾, there are two opinions.

One: the intended meaning is a command to declare the name of Allah free from defect and to sanctify it.

The second: "the name" (ism) is redundant (ṣila), and the intended meaning is a command to declare Allah Exalted free from defect.

On the first interpretation, the wording admits several possibilities.

The first: the intended meaning is, "Keep the name of your Lord free from being applied to anyone other than Him." This would then be a prohibition against naming anyone else by it, as the polytheists used to name an idol "al-Lāt" and Musaylima "Raḥmān al-Yamāma."

The second: that His names should not be explained by meanings that cannot validly be affirmed of Him, Glorified is He. An example is explaining "the Most High" (al-A'lā) as height in place, or "istiwā'" (settling) as "istiqrār" (fixing in place). Rather, "height" should be explained as dominance and power, and "istiwā'" as "istīlā'" (taking control).

The third: that the names should be protected from being cheapened and mentioned without reverence and magnification. This includes mentioning those names while heedless and without reflecting on their meanings and realities.

The fourth: that the meaning of "Glorify the name of your Lord" is: glorify Him by His names which I have sent down to you and informed you are His names, as in His words: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Gracious﴾ (al-Isrā' 17:110). A parallel to this interpretation is His words: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Most Great﴾ (al-Wāqi'a 56:74). The aim of this interpretation contains two points.

One: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾, that is, pray in the name of your Lord, not as the polytheists pray, with whistling and clapping.

Two: that the servant should not mention his Lord except by the names for which revelation has given authority (tawqīf) (scripturally attested terminology).

Al-Farrā' said: there is no difference between ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord﴾ and "Glorify with the name of your Lord." Al-Wāḥidī said: there is a difference between them, because the meaning of "Glorify with the name of your Lord" is: declare Allah free from defect by mentioning His name, which indicates His transcendence and exaltedness above what the falsifiers say. And ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord﴾ means: declare the name

[p. 124]

free from evil.

The fifth: Abū Muslim said: the meaning of "name" here is "attribute," and likewise in His words: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾ (al-A'rāf 7:180).

As for the second interpretation, that "name" is redundant and the meaning is "Glorify your Lord," which is the choice of a group of scholars who verify matters, they said: the name in reality is a word composed of letters, and it is not required to declare it free from defect as it is required for Allah Exalted. But when the one being mentioned is of utmost greatness, he himself is not mentioned; rather his name is mentioned, and it is said: "Glorify his name, and magnify his mention," as it is said: "Peace upon the exalted assembly." Labīd said:

*Until the year's end, then the name of peace be upon you both*

That is, "peace." This is a well-known usage in the language. On this view we say: glorifying Allah has two aspects.

The first: that one should not deal with the disbelievers in a way that leads them to mention Allah in an unseemly manner, as He said: ﴿And do not revile those whom they call upon besides Allah, lest they revile Allah in enmity without knowledge﴾ (al-An'ām 6:108).

The second: that it expresses declaring Allah Exalted free from everything unfitting for Him, in His essence, in His attributes, in His acts, in His names, and in His rulings. As for His essence: one should believe that it is not of the substances or accidents. As for His attributes: one should believe that they are not created, not finite, and not deficient. As for His acts: one should believe that He is the absolute owner, so no one has any objection to Him in any matter. The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) said: it means believing that whatever He does is good and right, that He does not do evil, and that He is not pleased with it. As for His names: He should not be mentioned except by names for which revelation has given authority. This is our position. But according to the Mu'tazila, it means He should not be mentioned except by names that do not imply deficiency in any respect, whether or not permission has been given for them. As for His rulings: one should know that He has not imposed obligations on us for a benefit returning to Himself, but either purely by His sovereign right, according to our view, or for the sake of preserving the interests of the servants, according to the view of the Mu'tazila.

**The second issue:** Some people have used this verse to argue that the name is identical with the named. I say: the discussion of the proof cannot be carried out except after clarifying the point of dispute. So it is necessary here to explain what the name is and what the named is, so that we can then discuss whether the name is the named or not. We say: if by "name" is meant this word, and by "named" is meant that essence, then the rational person cannot say: "The name is the named." If by "name" is meant that essence, and by "named" is also meant that essence, then our statement "the name is the named" amounts to saying that essence is that essence, and no rational person can dispute this. So we know that this issue, as presented, is weak. And if that is so, then pursuing a proof for it is even weaker and more remote. Rather, there is a subtle point here: our statement "name" means a word that we have made a name for everything that indicates a meaning not connected with time, and the name is like that, so it follows that the name is a name for itself. Here, then, the name is the named. Perhaps the earlier scholars mentioned this, and the matter became confused for later scholars, who assumed that in all contexts the name is the named. This is the essence of the verification in this issue. Let us return to the familiar discussion. They said: what shows that the name is the named is that no one says "Glory be to the name of Allah" or "Glory be to the name of our Lord." So the meaning of ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord﴾ is "Glorify your Lord," and "Lord" is also a name. If the name were other than the named, it would not be permissible for glorification to fall upon it. Know that this argument is weak, for, as we have explained in the first issue, it is possible that the command concerns glorifying the name itself. It is also possible that the intended meaning is glorifying the named, with "name" mentioned as a redundant element. It is also possible that the intended meaning is "Glorify with the name of your Lord," as in ﴿So glorify with the name of your Lord, the Most Great﴾, the meaning being "Glorify your Lord by mentioning His names."

[p. 125]

**The third issue:** It is narrated from 'Uqba ibn 'Āmir that when the words ﴿So glorify with the name of your Lord, the Most Great﴾ were revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to us: "Place it in your bowing (rukū')." And when the words ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ were revealed, he said: "Place it in your prostration (sujūd)." Then it is narrated in the reports that he (peace be upon him) used to say in his bowing: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great," and in his prostration: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High." Then some scholars said: these reports indicate that the intended meaning of ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord﴾ is "Pray in the name of your Lord." This possibility is strengthened by the consensus of the exegetes that His words ﴿So glory be to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ (al-Rūm 30:17) were revealed to explain the times of prayer.

**The fourth issue:** 'Alī (peace be upon him) and Ibn 'Umar read: "Glory be to the Most High, who created and proportioned." Perhaps the reason for this is that the word "Glorify" (sabbiḥ) is a command to glorify, so that glorification must be specified, and it is nothing other than the words: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High."

**The fifth issue:** Those who affirm bodily form (mujassima) (anthropomorphists) have used His words ﴿your Lord, the Most High﴾ to establish height in place. The truth is that height in direction is impossible for Allah Exalted. For He is either finite or infinite. If He is finite, then His upper extremity is finite, and there would be a direction above Him, and He, Glorified is He, would not be higher than all things. If He is infinite, then the existence of infinite dimensions is impossible. Furthermore, if He were infinite in all directions, His essence, Exalted is He, would have to be mixed with filth, Exalted is Allah above that. And if He were infinite in some directions and finite in others, the finite side would be different from the infinite side, so He would be composed of two parts. Everything composite is contingent, so the Necessary Existent in Himself would be contingent, and this is impossible. It is thus established that height here does not mean height in direction. What confirms this is that both what precedes this verse and what follows it are incompatible with the meaning of height in direction. As for what precedes the verse: height means being at the utmost distance from the world, and this does not fit the worthiness of glorification, praise, and exaltation. But height in the sense of perfection of power and sole creation and origination fits this. The sūra here is mentioned to describe Him with attributes for which He deserves praise, commendation, and magnification. As for what follows this verse: He follows the word "the Most High" with ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾, and creation corresponds to height in terms of power, not height in terms of direction.

* * *

**The sixth issue:** Some of the heretics (mulḥidūn) (those who deny God) have said that the Qur'an implies that the world has two lords, one of them great and the other higher than him. The great one is indicated by His words ﴿So glorify with the name of your Lord, the Most Great﴾, and the one higher than him by His words ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾. This, they argue, requires the existence of another lord of whom this one is higher.

Know that since the proofs have shown that the Creator, Exalted is He, is one, this objection falls. Then we say: this verse does not state that He, Glorified and Exalted is He, is higher than another lord. It says only that He is "the Most High." And we have several interpretations of it.

The first: He, Exalted is He, is higher, greater, and more magnificent than everything that those who describe Him describe Him with, and than every mention that those who remember Him make of Him. His majestic greatness is higher than our knowledge and perceptions, the kinds of His bounties and blessings are higher than our praise and gratitude, and the types of His rights are higher than our obedience and deeds.

The second: His words "the Most High" are a reminder that Allah deserves to be declared free from every deficiency. It is as if He said: "For He is the Most High," that is, He is exalted over everything by His dominion, sovereignty, and power. This is like saying: "I avoided wine, which removes reason," meaning: I avoided it because it removes reason.

The third: the intended meaning of "the Most High" is "the Exalted," just as the intended meaning of "the Greatest" is "the Great."

**The seventh issue:** It is narrated that he (peace be upon him) loved this sūra and used to say: "If people knew the value of 'Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High,' one of them would repeat it sixteen times." It is also narrated that 'Ā'isha passed by a Bedouin who was leading his companions in prayer, and he recited: "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who causes the pregnant woman to bring forth, who brings out from her a living soul that strives, from between the membranes and the belly. Is not that One able to give life to the dead? Yes indeed, yes indeed." Then 'Ā'isha said: "May your absent one not return, and may your women never cease to be in distress." And Allah knows best.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾ and ﴿who decreed and then guided﴾. Know that when He, glorified and exalted, commanded glorification (tasbih), it was as if a questioner said: "Engaging in glorification only comes after knowledge (ma'rifah). So what is the proof of the existence of the Lord?" Thus He said: ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾ and ﴿who decreed and then guided﴾. Know that reasoning from creation and guidance is the method relied upon by the greatest of the Prophets, peace be upon them, and the evidence for this is what God, exalted is He, related about Abraham, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 78]. And He related about Pharaoh that when he said to Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them both: ﴿So who is your Lord, O Moses?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 49], Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation and then guided it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50]. As for Muhammad (ﷺ), the first thing God, exalted is He, revealed to him was His saying: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ ﴿created man from a clinging substance﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1-2]. This is an indication of creation. Then He said: ﴿Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous﴾ ﴿who taught by the pen﴾ [al-'Alaq: 3-4]. This is an indication of guidance. Then God, exalted is He, repeated this argument in this surah, saying: ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾ ﴿and who decreed and then guided﴾. The reasoning by this method occurs frequently because, as we have mentioned, the wonders and marvels are greater in this method, and a person's witnessing of them and awareness of them is more complete; therefore they are stronger in indicating (the existence of the Creator). Then here there are several issues:

**First issue:** His saying, ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾, may be understood as referring specifically to humankind, or to animals, or to everything He created. Whoever understands it as referring to humankind mentions several meanings of "proportioning."

The first: He made his stature upright and balanced, and his form beautiful, as in His saying, ﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4]. He also praised Himself for having created him, saying, ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14].

The second: every animal is disposed to only one type of action and is not disposed to the rest of actions, whereas man was created in such a way that he can perform all the actions of animals through various instruments. Thus "proportioning" points to this.

The third: he was prepared for moral obligation (taklif) and for performing acts of worship.

As for whoever understands it as referring to all animals, he says: the meaning is that He gave every animal what it needs of organs, instruments and senses. We have fully discussed this topic in many places in this book.

As for whoever understands it as referring to all created things, he says: the meaning of "proportioning" is that He, exalted is He, is capable of all possibilities and knows all that is known. He created what He willed in accordance with what He willed, described by the quality of precision and perfection, free from defect and disorder.

**Second issue:** The majority (al-Jumhur) read *qaddara* with the doubled letter (shaddah). Al-Kisa'i read it without the doubling (*takhfif*). As for the doubled reading, the meaning is that He measured everything by a known measure. As for the light reading, al-Qaffal said: its meaning is "He possessed and guided." Its interpretation is: He created and proportioned, and He possessed what He created, meaning He disposed of it as He willed and wanted. This is ownership (al-milk), and "He guided it" means He guided it to its benefits and welfare. Some said: they are two dialects with one meaning. Among its examples is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So We measured, and excellent are the measurers﴾ [al-Mursalat: 23], read both with doubling and without.

[Page 127]

**Third issue:** His saying *qaddara* (measured) encompasses created things in their essences and attributes, each according to its own nature. He measured the heavens, the stars, the elements, the minerals, the plants, the animals and humankind with a specific measure of body and bulk. For each of them He determined a known duration of existence, and of attributes, colours, tastes, scents, forms, positions, beauty and ugliness, happiness and misery, guidance and error, a known measure, as in His saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasures, and We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾ [al-Hijr: 21]. The detailed explanation of this statement cannot be covered by volumes; indeed the whole world, from the highest of the 'Illiyyun to the lowest of the lowest, is the explanation of this verse, and the detail of this statement.

As for His saying *fahada* (and guided): the meaning is that every temperament (mizaj) is disposed to a particular power, and every power is suited only to a specific act. Thus "proportioning" and "measuring" are expressions for disposing the bodily parts and assembling them in a particular manner, by which they become ready to receive those powers. His saying *fahada* (guided) is an expression for creating those powers in those organs, such that each power becomes a source for a specific act, and from the totality of them the complete welfare is achieved.

The exegetes have several views on it. Muqatil said: He guided the male to the female, how he should approach her. Others said: He guided him to livelihood and cared for him. Others said: He guided man to the paths of good and evil, happiness and misery, because He made him perceptive, discerning, able to advance toward what pleases him and to refrain from what harms him, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, be he grateful or be he ungrateful﴾ [al-Insan: 3], and His saying: ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾ [al-Shams: 7–8]. Al-Suddi said: He measured the duration of the embryo in the womb, then guided it to emerge. Al-Farra' said: He measured and guided and misguided, and he suffices with mentioning one of them, as in His saying: ﴿Garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81]. Others said: *al-hidayah* here means calling to faith, as in His saying: ﴿And indeed you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura: 52], meaning you call. And all have been called to faith. Others said: He guided, meaning He indicated by His acts to His oneness, the majesty of His grandeur, the attributes of His self-sufficiency and His uniqueness, because the intelligent person sees in the world acts that are precise, perfect, coherent and well-ordered, which undoubtedly indicate an eternal Creator. Qatadah said regarding His saying *fahada*: Indeed Allah did not compel a servant to disobedience or to error, nor did He approve it for him or command him to it; rather He approved for you obedience, commanded you to it, and forbade you from disobedience.

Know that these views, despite their number, do not fall outside two categories. Some understood His saying *fahada* as relating to religion, as in His saying: ﴿And We guided him to the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10]. Others understood it as relating to the interests of the worldly life. The first is stronger, because His saying: ﴿He who created and proportioned﴾ and ﴿He who measured and guided﴾ refers to the affairs of this world, and the perfection of intellect and powers is included in it. Then He followed it with His saying *fahada* (guided), meaning He imposed obligation upon him and guided him to the religion.

As for His exalted saying: ﴿And He who brought out the pasture﴾, know that when He, glorified is He, explained what is specific to humankind, He followed it with mention of what is specific to non-humans among the blessings: He said: ﴿And He who brought out the pasture﴾, meaning He is the One capable of causing the herbage to grow, not the idols which the disbelievers worshipped. The *mar'a* (pasture) is what the earth brings forth of plants, fruits, crops and grass. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-mar'a* is green herbage. Then He said: ﴿Then He made it stubble, dark-green﴾. In this there are two issues:

**First issue:** *al-ghuthaʾ* (stubble) is what has dried of the plant, which torrents and waters carry away and winds scatter. Qutrub said: the singular of *al-ghuthaʾ* is *ghuthaʾah*.

**Second issue:** *al-hawwah* is blackness. Some said: *al-ahwa* is that which tends toward blackness when it is struck by moisture. Regarding *ahwa* there are two views. One: it is an attribute of *al-ghuthaʾ*, meaning that after being green it became dry and changed to blackness.

The meaning is: We shall make you a reciter of the Qur'an, who recites it and does not forget it. Mujahid, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: When the Qur'an was revealed to him, he would move his tongue a great deal out of fear that he would forget it, and Jibril would not finish the last of the revelation until he had spoken its beginning himself, out of fear of forgetting. Then they mentioned several ways in which this teaching and making-recite occurs.

One: Jibril, peace be upon him, will recite the Qur'an to you many times until you memorize it in a way that you will not forget.

Two: We will expand your breast and strengthen your memory, so that you memorize with a single time a memorization you will not forget.

Three: Since He commanded him at the beginning of the surah to glorify (Him), it is as if the Exalted said: Persist in that and continue upon it, for We shall make you recite the Qur'an, which comprises the knowledge of the first and the last, and in which is your mention and the mention of your people, and We shall gather it in your heart, and We shall make it easy for you to the ease (al-yusra), which is acting upon it.

**The second issue:** This verse indicates the miracle (mu'jizah) from two aspects.

The first: He was an unlettered man (ummi), and his memorization of this lengthy book without study, repetition or scribes is contrary to custom, and so it is a miracle.

The second: This surah is among the first things revealed in Mecca. Therefore, this is a report of a wondrous, strange matter, contrary to custom, that would occur in the future, and it did occur. So this is a report of the unseen, and thus a miracle.

As for His saying **"and you will not forget"**: some said that **"fa-la tansa"** means a prohibition, and the alif is added for the rhyme (fasila), like His saying **"the way"** (al-sabila) [al-Ahzab: 67]. The meaning is: do not neglect its recitation and repetition, lest you forget it, except what God wills that He cause you to forget. The well-known view, however, is that this is a statement (khabar), and the meaning is: We shall make you recite until you reach a state in which you will not forget and will be secure from forgetting, like your saying: "I will clothe you, so you will not be naked," meaning, so you will be secure from nakedness. Those who held this view argued against the weakness of the first view: that view is only complete if certain implications are accepted in this verse. Among them: forgetting is not within anyone's power except God's, so commands and prohibitions concerning it are not valid; therefore it must be interpreted as persistence in things that counter forgetting, such as study and frequent remembrance. All of that is a departure from the apparent wording. Among them: making the alif an addition for the rhyme, which is also contrary to the original form. Among them: if we take it as a statement, the meaning of the verse is God's good news to him that "I will make you such that you will not forget it." But if we take it as a prohibition, its meaning is that God commanded him to persist in the causes that prevent forgetting, namely study and recitation, and this is not in the nature of good news, and its exaltation of his state is not like the first. Moreover, it contradicts His saying: **"Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it"** [al-Qiyamah: 16].

As for His saying **"except what God wills,"** there are two possibilities.

One of them: it may be said that this exception does not actually occur, and that he, peace be upon him, did not forget anything after that. Al-Kalbi said: He, peace be upon him, did not forget anything after the revelation of this verse. On this interpretation, the purpose of His saying **"except what God wills"** is one of several matters:

One: the blessing (tabarruk) of mentioning this phrase, as the Exalted said: **"And never say of anything, 'Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,' unless (you add), 'If God wills'"** [al-Kahf: 23–24]. It is as if the Exalted says: Although I know all knowable things and know the outcomes of affairs in detail, I do not report the occurrence of anything in the future except with this phrase; so you, O Muhammad, and your community are more entitled to it.

Two: al-Farra' said: God did not will that Muhammad, peace be upon him, should forget anything. However, the purpose of mentioning this exception is to show that if God had willed that he become forgetful of it, He would have been able to do so, as He said: **"And if We willed, We could surely take away what We have revealed to you"** [al-Isra': 86]. Then we are certain that God did not will that, and He said to Muhammad, peace be upon him: **"If you associate others with God, your deeds will surely be lost"** [al-Zumar: 65], although he, peace and blessings be upon him, never associated anything with God at all. In sum, the benefit of this exception is that God makes him aware of His Lord's power, so that he knows that the absence of forgetting is from God's grace and kindness, not from his own strength.

Three: when the Exalted mentioned this exception, the Messenger of God ﷺ allowed that anything revealed to him, whether little or much, might be the one excepted. Therefore he would exert great effort in firmness, guarding and vigilance in all situations. So the purpose of mentioning this exception was that he, peace be upon him, remain vigilant in all circumstances.

Four: the purpose of His saying **"except what God wills"** may be the outright negation of forgetting, as a man says to his companion: "You are my partner in what I own, except in what God wills," without intending any actual exception.

One: al-Zajjaj said: except what God wills that he forget, for he forgets and then remembers afterward. So he may forget, but he remembers, and therefore he does not forget in a complete and permanent way. It is narrated that he dropped a verse in his recitation during prayer, and Ubayy thought it had been abrogated (nusikha), so he asked him, and he said: "I forgot it."

Two: Muqatil said: except what God wills to cause him to forget, and the meaning of "causing to forget" here is abrogation (nuskhah), as He said: **"Whatever verse We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or like it"** [al-Baqarah: 106]. For if he forgot something of the obligations and did not recall it, that would lead to a defect in the Law, and that is impermissible.

As for His saying, the Exalted: **"Indeed, He knows what is spoken aloud and what is hidden,"** there are two views.

One: the meaning is that He, glorified be He, knows your loud recitation alongside Jibril's recitation, and knows the secret in your heart, which is that you fear forgetting. So do not fear, for I will take care of what you fear.

Two: the meaning may be: "and you will not forget, except what God wills to abrogate, for He knows the interests of His servants best, so He abrogates where He knows that the interest lies in abrogation."

**Issue One:** As for His saying, ﴿And We will ease you toward ease﴾, there are several points. The first: *al-yusrā* (ease) refers to the deeds of goodness that lead to ease. Having understood this, we say that the *mufassirūn* (commentators on the Qur'an) have several views on it.

The first: His saying ﴿And We will ease you﴾ is connected to ﴿We will make you recite﴾, and His saying ﴿Indeed, He knows what is spoken aloud and what is hidden﴾ is a parenthetical clause. The meaning is: "We will make you recite, so you will not forget, and We will guide you to the method that is easiest and most facile," that is, in memorizing the Qur'an.

The second: Ibn Mas'ud said, "*al-yusrā* is Paradise," and the meaning is: "We will ease you toward the deed that leads to it."

The third: "We will make the Revelation easy for you, until you memorize it, learn it, and act upon it."

The fourth: "We will guide you to the *sharī'ah* (sacred law), which is the *ḥanīfiyyah* (pure monotheistic way), easy and tolerant." The first view is closer to the truth.

**Issue Two:** A questioner may ask: the customary expression is to say, "such-and-such act was made easy (*juʻila al-fiʻl al-fulānī muyassaran*) for so-and-so," and one does not say, "so-and-so was made easy (*juʻila fulānun muyassaran*) for such-and-such act." So what is the benefit of the phrasing here?

The answer: just as this expression is the choice of the Qur'an in this passage and also in Surah al-Layl, so too it is the choice of the Messenger (ﷺ) in his saying, peace be upon him: "Act, for each is made easy for that for which he was created." There is a subtle scientific point in this. That act, in itself, is a possible reality (*māhiyyah mumkinah*) that is equally receptive to existence and non-existence. So long as the capable agent remains equally balanced with respect to doing and not doing the act, the act cannot proceed from him. When the side of agency (*fā'iliyyah*) is given preference over the side of abandoning (*tārikiyyah*), then the act comes into being. Thus it is established that the act does not come about unless it becomes necessary, and that preponderance is what is called *tayseer* (facilitation). Therefore it is established that the truth of the matter is that the agent becomes *muyassar* (made easy) for the act, not that the act becomes *muyassar* for the agent. Glory be to Him, under every word of Whose is a hidden wisdom and a wondrous secret that dazzles the minds.

**Issue Three:** He said, ﴿And We will ease you toward ease﴾ using the plural of majesty (*nūn al-ta'ẓīm*), so that the greatness of the Giver would indicate the greatness of the gift. Its parallel is His saying, ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 9] and ﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar﴾ [al-Kawthar: 1]. This verse indicates that He, glory be to Him, opened to him, from the doors of facilitation and ease, what He did not open to anyone else. And how could it not be so, when he was an orphan child, with neither father nor mother, raised among an ignorant people? Then He, exalted is He, made him in his deeds and sayings a model for all the worlds, and a guidance for all creation.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 87, verse 9:

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾

Know that when Almighty God had undertaken to facilitate all the interests of this world and the Hereafter, He commanded the calling of creation to the Truth (al-Haqq), because the perfection of a human being's state lies in his being characterized by the character traits of God, glorified is He, completely and beyond completeness. So when Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace, became complete, in accordance with His saying: ﴿And We will ease you toward ease﴾, He commanded him to make himself beyond completeness, in accordance with His saying: "So remind," because reminding requires the completion of the deficient and the guidance of the ignorant, and whoever is like that is an overflowing source of perfection. Thus he was complete and beyond completeness. Here there are questions.

The first question: He, upon him be peace, was sent to all people, so it is obligatory for him to remind them whether or not the reminder benefits them. What then is meant by making it conditional in His saying: ﴿if the reminder benefits﴾? The answer: that what is made conditional with "in" (in, "if") on something does not necessarily become nonexistent when that thing is absent. Evidence for this includes this verse, and His saying: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution if they desire chastity﴾ [al-Nur: 33]; and His saying: ﴿And be thankful to God, if it is Him you worship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172]; and His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer if you fear﴾ [al-Nisa: 101], for shortening is permissible even when fear is not present; and His saying: ﴿And if you find no scribe, then a pledge﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283], for pledging is permissible together with writing; and His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon them if they return to one another, if they think that they will keep the limits of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230], for returning is permissible without this assumption. Having understood this, we say: they mentioned several benefits for mentioning this condition:

The first: whoever undertakes an act for a purpose, there is no doubt that the case in which it is known that this means leads to that purpose is more compelling for that act than the case in which it is known that this leading does not occur. Therefore He said: ﴿if the reminder benefits﴾.

The second: He mentioned the more noble of the two states and alluded to the other, as in His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾, and the implied meaning is: ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits, or does not benefit﴾.

The third: that what is meant by it is urging them to benefit from the reminder, as a person says to another when he has made the truth clear to him: "I have made it clear to you, if you understand," so his intent is to urge him to accept it and benefit from it.

The fourth: that this operates as an alert to the Messenger ﷺ that the reminder will not benefit them, as one says to a man: "Call so-and-so, if he answers you," meaning: "I do not think he will answer you."

The fifth: that he, upon him be peace, called them to God many times, and whenever his calling became more frequent, their rebellion became greater, and he, upon him be peace, would be consumed with grief over this. So it was said to him: ﴿And you are not over them a compeller. So remind with the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾ [Qaf: 45], since general reminding is obligatory at the beginning of the matter, but repetition is perhaps obligatory only when there is hope of achieving the intended aim; for this reason He restricted it with this condition.

The second question: making something conditional is only fitting for one who is ignorant of outcomes, but how is that fitting for the Knower of the unseen? The answer: it is reported in the books that He, exalted is He, said to Musa: ﴿So speak to him gently; perhaps he will remember or fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44], and I testify that he will neither remember nor fear. The command of calling and sending is one thing, and His knowledge of the unseen and the outcomes of affairs is another, and it is not possible to build one of them upon the other.

The third question: is the reminding commanded here fixed, such as reminding them tens of times, or is it not fixed? In that case, how is one discharged from the obligation of the duty? The answer: the criterion for it is custom ('urf). And God knows best.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He who fears will be reminded﴾

There are several issues here.

The first issue: know that people's positions regarding the return (al-ma'ad, the Resurrection) fall into three categories. Some are certain of its truth. Some consider its occurrence possible but are not certain about it, neither denying nor affirming it. Others insist on denying it and are certain that it will not happen. The first two categories are those in whom fear is present, whereas the third has no fear and no dread. Once you know this, it becomes clear that the verse admits of two interpretations.

One: it may be said that the one who fears is the one who knows God and knows the perfection of His power, knowledge and wisdom. This requires that he be certain of the truth of the Resurrection. For this reason, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ [Fatir: 28]. It is as if, when He said, ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾, He then explained in this verse who it is that benefits from the reminder. Since benefiting from the reminder depends on the presence of fear in the heart, and the states of hearts are something no one can perceive except God, glory be to Him, it became incumbent upon the Messenger to generalize the call in order to attain the objective, for the objective is to remind those who benefit from reminding, and there is no way to reach them except by generalizing the reminder.

Two: it may be said that fear is present in those who act (on the message) and in those who hesitate without being obstinate. Most people are hesitant and not obstinate, and the obstinate among them are few. When the hesitant, who form the majority, are combined with those who know, the great majority becomes non-obstinate. Moreover, many of the obstinate oppose only with their tongues. As for one who is obstinate in his heart, within himself, that is something that either does not occur or, if it does, is extremely rare. Furthermore, when a person hears the warning that he will ﴿burn in the greatest Fire﴾ and that he ﴿will neither die therein nor live﴾, his heart is broken, and so it is inevitable that most people, in most circumstances, will listen and benefit. As for that one who turns away, he is rare, and abandoning a great good for the sake of a small evil is itself a great evil. On this basis, His saying ﴿So remind, if the reminder benefits﴾ requires the generalization of the reminder.

The third issue: the sīn in His saying ﴿sa-yadhdhakkaru﴾ may carry the meaning of "sawfa yadhdhakkaru" (he will surely be reminded), and the "sawfa" coming from God is binding, like His saying ﴿We shall make you recite, and you will not forget﴾. It is also possible that the meaning is that whoever fears God will be reminded, even if after some time, through the reflection and consideration he undertakes; he will be reminded after a long period. And God knows best.

The fourth issue: knowledge is only called "remembrance" (tadhakkur) if knowledge had first been acquired and then forgotten. This state does not apply to the unbelievers, so how did God call this remembrance? The answer is that because the proofs are so strong and manifest, it is as if that knowledge had been present, and then it departed due to imitation (taqlid) and obstinacy. For this reason God named it remembrance.

The fifth issue: it has been said that this verse was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Affan, and it has been said that it was revealed concerning Ibn Umm Maktum.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 87, verses 11–12:

As for His saying, ﴿And the most wretched will avoid it﴾ ﴿who will burn in the greatest Fire﴾: know that we have explained that people fall into three categories: the knowers, the hesitant, and the obstinate deniers. We have also explained that the first two categories must have fear and dread, and the one who has dread must listen to the call and benefit from it. So the most wretched is the obstinate one who neither listens to the call nor benefits from it. Therefore God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the most wretched will avoid it﴾ ﴿who will burn in the greatest Fire﴾. On this there are two issues:

The first issue: They have mentioned several interpretations of ﴿the greatest Fire﴾:

One of them: Al-Hasan (al-Hasan al-Basri) said: "The greatest (al-Kubra) is the Fire of Jahannam, and the lesser (al-Sughra) is the fire of this world."

The second: In the Hereafter there are fires and degrees that differ, just as in this world there are sins and disobediences that differ. Just as the disbeliever is the most wretched of the sinners, so he will burn in the greatest of the fires.

The third: The greatest Fire is the lowest Fire (al-Nar al-Sufla), and it afflicts the disbelievers, as He said: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire﴾ [an-Nisa: 145].

[p. 133]

The second issue: They said: This verse was revealed concerning al-Walid, Utbah and Ubayy. You know that the lesson (al-'ibrah) is drawn from the generality of the wording (ʿumum al-lafz), not from the particularity of the occasion of revelation (khusus al-sabab), especially since we have demonstrated the correctness of this order by rational proof.

The third issue: Someone may say: God, exalted is He, has mentioned here two categories: one who takes heed and fears, and the second, the most wretched, who will burn in the greatest Fire. But the existence of "the most wretched" requires the existence of "the wretched," so what is the state of this category?

The answer: The word "the most wretched" (al-ashqa) does not require the existence of a "wretched" (al-shaqi), since this kind of expression may be used without any sharing, as in His saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day will have a better dwelling and a finer resting place﴾ [al-Furqan: 24]. It has also been said that the meaning is: "And the wretched one who will burn will avoid it," as in His saying: ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾ [ar-Rum: 27], i.e., easy for Him, and like the saying of the poet:

"Indeed He who raised the heaven built for us a house whose pillars are mightier and taller."

This is what has been said. But the verified view is what we have mentioned: the three groups are the knower, the hesitant, and the obstinate. The happy one is the knower, the hesitant has some share of wretchedness, and the most wretched is the obstinate one, whom we have shown to be the one who does not turn toward the call, does not incline to it, and avoids it. ﴿Then he will neither die therein nor live﴾ ﴿He has succeeded who purifies himself﴾.

Regarding His saying, ﴿Then he will neither die therein nor live﴾, there are two issues.

The first issue: the exegetes have two views concerning it.

One of them: he will not die and thus find rest, nor will he live a life that benefits him, as He said: ﴿Its punishment will not be decreed for them so that they die, nor will its torment be lightened for them﴾ [Fatir: 36]. This is according to the manner of the Arabs, who say of one afflicted with severe affliction: "He is neither alive nor dead."

The second: its meaning is that the soul of one of them in the Fire becomes lodged in his throat, so it does not come out and he dies, nor does it return to its place in the body and he lives.

The second issue: the word "thumma" (then) is used because this state is more dreadful and greater than the burning fire; it is thus remote from it in degrees of severity.

Regarding His saying, ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself﴾, there are two views:

One of them: when He mentioned the threat against those who turn away from reflecting and contemplating the proofs of Allah, He followed it with the promise for those who purify themselves and cleanse themselves from the filth of polytheism.

The second, which is the view of al-Zajjaj: "he increases in piety," because the meaning of "zakī" is "one who grows and is abundant." This view is supported by His saying: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded, those who are humble in their prayer﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1], where He affirmed success for those who combine those qualities; likewise His saying at the beginning of al-Baqarah: ﴿And it is those who are the successful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5].

As for the first view, it is supported by two points:

The first: since He did not mention in the verse what one must purify oneself from, we know that the intended meaning is purification from what was mentioned before the verse, and that is disbelief. So we know that the intended meaning here, ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself﴾, is purification from the disbelief that was mentioned before this verse.

The second: the unrestricted term refers to the complete form of the thing named, and the most complete kind of purification is the purification of the heart from the darkness of disbelief, so this unrestricted term must be understood in that sense. This interpretation is reinforced by what is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, that he said the meaning of "tazakkā" is the saying: "There is no god but Allah."

Regarding His saying, ﴿And remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: The scholars of tafsir mentioned several views concerning it:

The first of them: Ibn 'Abbas said: he remembered his return (ma'ad) and his standing before his Lord, and so he prayed to Him. I say: this interpretation is the one that is definite, because the stages of the actions of the mukallaf (the responsible person) are three:

The first of them: removing corrupt beliefs from the heart.

The second of them: bringing to mind the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, with respect to His essence, attributes and names.

The third of them: occupying oneself with His service.

The first stage is what is meant by purification (tazkiyah) in His saying: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself﴾.

The second is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And remembers the name of his Lord﴾, for remembrance by the heart is nothing but knowledge (ma'rifah).

The third is service, which is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and prays﴾, for prayer (salah) is an expression of humility and submissiveness. Whoever's heart is illuminated by knowledge of the majesty and greatness of Allah, the Exalted, the effect of submission and humility must appear in his limbs and organs.

The second view: some of the scholars of tafsir said that His saying, ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself﴾, means: whoever gives charity before going out to the 'Eid. ﴿And remembers the name of his Lord and prays﴾ means: then he prays the 'Eid prayer afterwards with the imam. This is the view of 'Ikrimah, Abu al-'Aliyah, Ibn Sirin and Ibn 'Umar, and this was narrated as a marfu' report to the Prophet ﷺ. This interpretation has a problem from two aspects:

The first: the habit of Allah in the Qur'an is to mention prayer before zakat, not to mention zakat before prayer.

The second: al-Tha'labi said: this surah is Meccan by consensus, and there was no 'Eid nor zakat al-fitr in Mecca. al-Wahidi answered him that it is not impossible to say: since it was within the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, that this would occur, He praised the one who did it.

The third view: Muqatil said: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself﴾ means he gave charity from his wealth, and remembered his Lord with monotheism in the prayer, and so prayed to Him. The difference between this view and the previous one is that this includes the obligatory zakat and the obligatory prayer, whereas the first view does not.

The fourth view: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself﴾ does not mean the zakat of wealth, but the purification of deeds, i.e., one who purifies his deeds from showing off and shortcoming, because the customary wording for wealth is "zakka" and one does not say "tazakka" in that sense. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever purifies himself, he purifies only for himself﴾ [Fatir: 18].

The fifth view: Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿And remembers the name of his Lord﴾ means he glorified God (kabbara) as he went out to the 'Eid and prayed the 'Eid prayer.

The sixth view: the meaning is: he remembered the name of his Lord in his prayer, and his prayer is not like the prayer of the hypocrites, who show off to people and do not remember Allah except a little.

The second issue: The jurists (fuqaha') used this verse as evidence for the obligation of the opening takbir (takbirat al-ifitah, the first takbir that opens the prayer). Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, used it to argue that the opening takbir is not part of the prayer. He said: because the prayer is conjoined to it (ma'tuf 'alayha), and conjunction requires difference. He also used this verse to argue that opening the prayer is permissible with any of Allah's names. Our companions answered that the implied sense of the verse is: "and prayed, so he remembered the name of his Lord," and there is no difference between saying "you honored me so you visited me" and saying "you visited me so you honored me." Abu Hanifah could reply: abandoning the function of the fa' of sequence (ta'qib) is not permitted without evidence. The better answer is to say: the verse indicates the praise of everyone who remembers the name of Allah and prays immediately after it, and the verse does not state that this remembrance is the opening takbir. Perhaps what is meant is that whoever remembers Allah in his heart, and recalls His reward and punishment, is moved by that to perform the prayer, and then he performs the prayer one of whose parts is the takbir; and in that case the argument is refuted.

Then God Most High says: ﴿Rather, you prefer the worldly life﴾. There are two readings of this. The reading of the majority (al-'ammah) is with the "ta" (tu'thirūna, the second person), and the letter of Ubayy (Ubayy ibn Ka'b's codex) reinforces it, meaning: "Rather, you yourselves prefer the work of this world over the work of the Hereafter." Ibn Mas'ud said: "The world was brought forward, and its food, drink, women, pleasures and splendor were hastened to us, while the Hereafter is unseen to us and was hidden from us, so we took what is immediate and left what is deferred." Abu 'Amr read "yu'thirūna" with the "ya", meaning: the wretched (al-ashqā).

Then God Most High says: ﴿And the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾.
Its completion is that whatever is better and more enduring is more worthy of preference (ātharu), so it follows that the Hereafter is more worthy of preference than this world, while they were preferring this world. We have said that the Hereafter is better for several reasons:

The first: the Hereafter comprises bodily and spiritual happiness, whereas the world is not like that. So the Hereafter is better than the world.

The second: the pleasures of this world are mixed with pains, whereas the Hereafter is not like that.

The third: this world is perishing, and the Hereafter is everlasting, and the everlasting is better than the perishing.

Then He says: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures﴾. They differed concerning what is indicated by the word "this" (hadhā). Some said: it is the entire surah, because the surah comprises monotheism (tawhīd), prophethood, a warning against disbelief in God, and a promise for obedience to God Most High.
Others said: rather, what is indicated by this demonstrative is His saying: ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies himself﴾, as an indication of the purification of the soul from everything that is not fitting.
